title: Connelly v. United States, 602 U.S. 257 (2024), No. 23-146 (preliminary print of the opinion)
publisher: Supreme Court of the United States (supremecourt.gov)
claims: Connelly v. United States was decided June 6, 2024, with Justice Thomas delivering the opinion for a unanimous Court affirming the Eighth Circuit.

The Court described the facts as two brothers who were the sole shareholders of a closely held corporation and had an agreement under which the surviving brother had the option to purchase a deceased brother's shares and, if he declined, the corporation was required to redeem them, and the corporation obtained 3.5 million dollars in life insurance on each brother to fund a possible redemption.

The Court stated that the decedent owned 77.18 percent of the corporation's shares, that his son and the surviving brother agreed the shares were worth 3 million dollars rather than obtaining the outside appraisal the agreement contemplated, and that the corporation used 3 million dollars of the life-insurance proceeds to redeem them.

The Court stated that the estate's valuation excluded the 3 million dollars of insurance proceeds used for the redemption and valued the corporation at 3.86 million dollars, while the IRS counted those proceeds, valued the corporation at 6.86 million dollars and the decedent's shares at 5.3 million dollars, and determined that the estate owed an additional 889,914 dollars in tax.

The Court stated that all parties agreed that life-insurance proceeds payable to a corporation are an asset that increases the corporation's fair market value, and that the only question was whether the corporation's contractual obligation to redeem the decedent's shares at fair market value offsets the value of life-insurance proceeds committed to funding that redemption.

The Court held that the corporation's contractual obligation to redeem the decedent's shares did not diminish the value of those shares, and that redemption obligations are not necessarily liabilities that reduce a corporation's value for purposes of the federal estate tax.

The Court reasoned that a share redemption at fair market value does not affect any shareholder's economic interest, and that for calculating the estate tax the point is to assess how much the shares were worth at the time of death, before the corporation spent the insurance proceeds on the redemption.

In a footnote the Court stated that it did not hold that a redemption obligation can never decrease a corporation's value, giving as an example an obligation that requires a corporation to liquidate operating assets to pay for the shares, and stated that it rejected only the position that all redemption obligations reduce a corporation's net value.
The Court stated that a share redemption agreement ordinarily is not dispositive for valuing a decedent's shares for the estate tax, citing 26 U.S.C. 2703.

Responding to the argument that its holding would make succession planning more difficult, the Court stated that the result was a consequence of how the brothers chose to structure their agreement and that there were other options, giving as an example a cross-purchase agreement, in which shareholders agree to purchase each other's shares at death and purchase life-insurance policies on each other to fund the agreement.

The Court accepted as true enough the petitioner's argument that, if proceeds earmarked for a redemption are a net asset for estate tax purposes, the corporation would have needed an insurance policy worth far more than 3 million dollars to redeem the decedent's shares at fair market value.

The Court stated that a cross-purchase agreement would have let the surviving brother buy the shares while avoiding the risk that the insurance proceeds would increase the value of the decedent's shares, because the proceeds would have gone directly to him rather than to the corporation.

The Court stated that every arrangement has its own drawbacks: a cross-purchase agreement would have required each brother to pay the premiums on the policy on the other, creating a risk that one would be unable to do so, and would have had its own tax consequences, while the corporation's ownership of the policies ensured they would remain in force but meant the corporation would receive the proceeds and thereby increase the value of the decedent's shares.

The Court's opinion notes that not all estates are subject to the estate tax and that, because of credits allowed against the tax, an estate valued below a threshold the Court described as about 13.6 million dollars at the time is not subject to it, citing 26 U.S.C. 2010(c).
updateCadence: A decided case does not change, but this is a preliminary print subject to formal revision before the bound volume is published. Later legislation or regulation could change the law the case applied.
notes: The holding is about a redemption agreement, under which the corporation itself buys the shares with proceeds it receives. The Court's remarks on cross-purchase agreements describe an alternative the parties could have used and the Court's view of its tradeoffs; the Court did not decide a case about a cross-purchase agreement. The estate tax threshold figure is the Court's own approximation at the time of the opinion and is not a current figure. Nothing here states how any reader's agreement would be valued or taxed.
